title: Firouzja, Caruana, Giri, MVL Win Groups; Carlsen's No. 1 Status Boosted By Caruana Loss
summary:
It's GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave vs. GM Anish Giri and GM Fabiano Caruana vs. GM Alireza Firouzja in the Semifinals of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026 after the four players won their groups. Caruana wrapped up victory with a round to spare, while Giri and Firouzja eased home with two draws. The drama came in Group D, where a last-minute win for GM Vaishali Rameshbabu gave Vachier-Lagrave the top spot instead of GM Arjun Erigaisi, while at one point it seemed GM Hans Niemann could even win the group as he hit back to beat GM Wesley So.

There was a lot of following other games as the final spots in the knockout were decided. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

GM Magnus Carlsen remained winless in fast classical after missing a great chance against GM Ian Nepomniachtchi in a game where he'd also potentially been in trouble on move 11. Two draws kept Carlsen above 2800—just—while there was some good news for his number-one spot when Caruana lost his final game to GM Vladislav Artemiev. That returned GM Hikaru Nakamura to the world number-two spot, 9.2 points behind Carlsen. That gap could close fast, however, if Carlsen doesn't win his games against GM Bibisara Assaubayeva in the knockout for 17th place.

Day seven, the first of the Knockout Stage, starts after the rest day, on Tuesday, November 17, at 9 a.m. ET / 15:00 CET / 7:30 p.m. IST.

Group A: Firouzja's Gamble Pays Off

Group B: Caruana Wins With Round To Spare, Then Loses 1st Game

Group C: Giri Eases To Victory, Carlsen Ends Winless

Group D: MVL Wins After Vaishali Shocks Arjun

Knockout Brackets

Group Stage Round 9 Results

There was a sea of draws in the penultimate round, except in Group D.

It was similar again in the final round, with Group D bringing the drama, with all three games won by White.

Group Stage Round 10 Results

Group A: Firouzja's Gamble Pays Off

Group A Final Standings

Firouzja came into the final day as group leader and completed his task with the minimum of fuss, making two quick draws against GM Levon Aronian. Firouzja is enjoying the faster classical games, and had a surprising suggestion: "Maybe they should make the time control a bit shorter—it’s almost the same, 15 minutes difference, not a big deal!"

Maybe they should make the time control a bit shorter.

—Alireza Firouzja

Alireza Firouzja played solidly and challenged his rivals to catch him. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Firouzja's second draw was something of a gamble, since GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda had given himself a chance to take first with a sparkling win over GM Jorden van Foreest in the first game.

If Duda won again, he would snatch the top spot in the group, but Firouzja reasoned, "If Duda wins 2-0 against Jorden, he just deserves it!"

Duda and Van Foreest after the first game. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

The problem for Duda was that Van Foreest explained afterward that he was "fine with a draw" that would seal the third spot in the group for him. Duda didn't know how to play for a win with Black, but tried anyway, only to slip into a worse endgame and gradually get ground down. He explained the games being rated as classical was also a factor, since if they weren't rated, "I would go crazy to win the game with Black."

Duda still took second on the tiebreak of scoring better in the earlier blitz tournament, Van Foreest was third, Aronian fourth, and, after two draws in their encounter, GM Andrew Hong took fifth and GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov a shocking last place—though the world number-five was far from the only star player to suffer in Budapest.

Abdusattorov suffered in the blitz and then couldn't recover in fast classical. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Group B: Caruana Wins With Round To Spare, Then Loses 1st Game

Group B Final Standings

This was the group with the least intrigue, since Caruana entered with a four-point lead, while GM Liem Le needed only to avoid losses to seal second place. Le was happy to take a draw in the first game against GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, which confirmed Caruana as the group winner even while his clash with Artemiev continued.

Le could only mathematically catch Caruana with two wins, but settled for an early draw. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Caruana missed a win which would have put him above 2800 and within 0.8 rating points of Carlsen, but could relax for the second game. He visited the confessional to say he was "messing around a bit" in the second game to keep winning chances.

Caruana decides to tick off one of his obligatory confessionals now that he's wrapped up victory in his group — he says he's "messing around a bit because I do want to create some chances for a win" vs. Artemiev! #TotalChess https://t.co/E2GweX442i

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 15, 2026

In hindsight, that proved a mistake, since the winless Artemiev finally showed his teeth and scored a fine win, seizing control of the center, forcing the win of material, and then smoothly converting.

That loss took some of the sheen off a near-perfect performance from Caruana, and cost him 6.8 rating points, taking him back down below Nakamura on the live rating list.

The fast classical games have wrought havoc with the rating list, and there are still four more games for every player.

Elsewhere in the group the games were drawn, with GM Vincent Keymer celebrating his 22nd birthday by making a great rook-endgame escape in the first game against GM Richard Rapport. Rapport still took third ahead of Keymer, while world number-seven Praggnanandhaa finished last and will, remarkably, now face fellow giant Abdusattorov in the Semifinals of the knockout for 21st place.

Vincent Keymer escapes with a draw on his birthday. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

He commented: "I would, first of all, like to finish off the event, but it’s not possible, because you still have to play. It doesn’t matter if you finish sixth in the group stage, you still have to play, which is honestly sad!"

It doesn't matter if you finish sixth in the group stage, you still have to play, which is honestly sad!

—Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu

Group C: Giri Eases To Victory, Carlsen Ends Winless

Group C Final Standings

If Praggnanandhaa and Abdusattorov suffering is a shock, it's no less than seeing Carlsen, who most felt the whole tournament format should favor, ending the group stage without a single win—and with a 21.8-point rating loss.

It wasn't for want of trying, with the first game against Nepomniachtchi simply wild. Carlsen took big risks in the opening, but then seized his biggest advantage of the whole tournament. His enemy, yet again, however, was the clock.

Here there was no reason for Carlsen not to grab the pawn on b2, while after 26...Bd8?! 27.Rh2 the game was in the balance again.

Anything could have happened, with Carlsen standing on the precipice of losing his 15-year unbroken streak as world number-one if he lost (before Caruana drew), while Nepomniachtchi also needed a win for the top spot in the group. "Being slightly ahead on the clock, I wanted to get a messy position, and eventually it worked out more or less decently!" Nepomniachtchi commented, and he was the player who could choose to play on at the end. There was no clear path to an advantage, however, so he forced a draw.

Carlsen has had some very lively classical games and post-mortems, but so far no wins. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

That's our Game of the Day, which GM Rafael Leitao has analyzed below.

The second game was also tense, with Carlsen suddenly injecting life into what had seemed a dead-equal position by targeting the black king.

It only led to an endgame with a slight edge for White, however, and Nepomniachtchi held without the slightest trouble.

That meant Giri won the group with two relatively fast draws against GM Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, with GM Haik Martirosyan third and only GM Abhimanyu Mishra in last place below fifth-placed Carlsen.

Mishra and Martirosyan canceled each other out. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

After winning the group, Giri described the format as "a fun time control," but said it remained a question whether it should be rated as classical. He didn't want the organizers to pay too much attention to complaints, however, and warmed to his theme as he added:

I remember all this internet crowd was always for faster games, for the death of classical chess, and now suddenly people changed, it’s a big outrage, the silent classical majority has risen from the dead and suddenly everyone loves classical chess. Even Hikaru and all these people. Where were they when we needed them so much, when there’s a world championship match, one game a day? Basically they hate no matter what you do, so as organizers you have to really think, evaluate, and not get carried away by some social media posts... Have it clear in your mind what it is that you want, what are your values, what have your parents taught you? The organizers should look in the mirror—would my mother be proud of me? Rather than trying to go after the mob, which is absolutely impossible to satisfy.

The silent classical majority has risen from the dead and suddenly everyone loves classical chess.

—Anish Giri

Anish Giri won Group C. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

That leaves us with Group D, which was by far the day's most dramatic.

Group D: MVL Wins After Vaishali Shocks Arjun

Group D Final Standings

Only Vachier-Lagrave went into the final day with his fate in his own hands in this group, where three players were tied for first place. As the runner-up in the blitz, the Frenchman had the best tiebreak, so he knew that two wins over Assaubayeva would seal first place. That wasn't to be, however, since he was held to a draw in the first, explaining, "Bibisara defended tenaciously, found some good moves, and I couldn’t see what else to do."

Maxime Vachier-Lagrave's draw and win against Assaubayeva proved to be enough. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

That was a chance for the other leaders, but Niemann fell to So when he blundered with 59...f4? in a position he'd disliked since going astray in the opening.

In the post-game interview, So referred to something he'd said about Niemann four years ago at the U.S. Championship:

I’ve got no beef against Hans. I think many years ago I said he’s the most disrespectful teenager in chess, but he’s no longer a teenager, so I’d like to apologize for that comment. I wish Hans nothing but the best with his chess career. I really hope he gets a successful chess career, or whatever he does in life. He’s a good kid!

I've got no beef against Hans.

—Wesley So

Wesley So won the first game against Hans Niemann. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

In the same interview, however, So did have a beef against the tournament format, since he was just learning that they'd play seven or eight games at different time controls each day during the knockout stage. "It seems like someone really hates us players, that someone’s trying to kill us!" he commented, before expanding on the topic on X.

Whoever designed the Total Pilot format deserves an award, a bonus, and a salary raise. Playing 8 games a day, different time controls, 4 days straight in the match stage is maximum absurdity. At some point, you have to wonder whether this is a chess tournament or a military endurance test. Please pray for my health 🙏🤲

— Wesley So (@WesleySo_) November 15, 2026

Meanwhile, the other co-leader at the start of the day, Arjun, did manage to overcome Vaishali, meaning he'd taken the sole lead and now had his fate in his own hands.

The drama only increased in the second games of the day, however. Niemann managed to bounce back against So, and briefly it seemed he might pull off an astonishing group win, since both Vachier-Lagrave and Arjun were struggling. Soon, however, Vachier-Lagrave said he "found some trick" and managed to beat Assaubayeva, so it was all down to Vaishali vs. Arjun.

title: Nakamura's Best Bullet Brawl Year Gets Even Better With 74th Title
summary:
GM Hikaru Nakamura gained his 74th win in the Bullet Brawl arena on Saturday, cruising to 178 points and winning by a commanding 21-point margin, all the while singing along to background music and entertaining viewers on Kick.

GM Jeffery Xiong took second place, while IM Renato Terry and GM Tuan Minh Le secured third and fourth with 143 and 136 points, respectively. Meanwhile, WIM Melika Mohammadi scored 103 points and will receive the $100 best women's prize.

The next edition of Bullet Brawl will begin on Saturday, November 21, at 12 p.m. ET / 18:00 CET / 10:30 p.m. IST.

(Full final standings here.)

A total of 235 titled players participated in Saturday's arena, which featured Nakamura alongside GMs Xiong, Le, Parham Maghsoodloo, Volodar Murzin, Oleksandr Bortnyk, and Haowen Xue. The strength of the field seemed to matter little to the now-74-time victor, who won his first 13 games and seized the lead without breaking a sweat.

Nakamura is scarcely caught after such a strong start.

FM Prokhor Moskvinov became one of the world number-three's victims during the stretch, falling to the trenchant 25...Rxf3!!, which shredded the redoubt around his king.

Soon after, Nakamura faced his greatest challenge on paper yet in GM Jose Martinez. However, the American was gifted a free bishop on the 24th move after his opponent failed to find a precise defensive move.

Nakamura's winning streak was eventually snapped by Xiong, who had emerged as a contender despite suffering consecutive defeats early. At the halfway mark, Nakamura held a 19-point advantage over Xiong, while 16 more points separated the latter from the third-placed Le.

While bopping along to background beats, Nakamura continued his dominance in the second half. Although players occasionally managed a scalp against the format's GOAT, he never lost back-to-back games.

Nakamura was fairly casual for most of the arena, but did get serious when push came to shove. Image: GMHikaru/Kick.

Xiong, who was responsible for three of Nakamura's defeats, proved to be his most formidable opponent. Nevertheless, by the end of the arena, Nakamura had established an 8-3 head-to-head score. In their third-to-last game, Xiong threw in the towel after Nakamura had built an 11-second advantage and capitalized on a positional mistake on move 36.

Xiong focused on getting through a high volume of games to make up for the lopsided head-to-head score, though even 10 extra games weren't enough. Nakamura finished the arena with a remarkable 51 wins, three draws, and just seven losses in two hours.

Simply indomitable.

With this victory, Nakamura has extended his record-breaking tally of calendar-year Bullet Brawl victories to 25, accounting for just over half of the editions held so far this year. Even more impressively, he has finished outside the winner's circle in just two editions in which he has participated, securing second place on both occasions.

title: Firouzja, Caruana, Giri and Vachier-Lagrave win groups in Budapest
summary: Vaishali defeats Erigaisi as Artemiev ends Caruana’s unbeaten Fast Classic run Alireza Firouzja, Fabiano Caruana, Anish Giri and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave secured the four places in the championship knockout bracket as the Fast Classic group stage of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot concluded in Budapest. Vaishali Rameshbabu defeated Arjun Erigaisi in the return game, while Vladislav Artemiev handed Caruana his first defeat of the group stage. Games 9 and 10 produced eight decisive results from 24 encounters, all won by White. Each player faced the same opponent twice with colours reversed, with three points awarded for a win and one for a draw. Firouzja holds on as Duda and Van Foreest exchange wins Alireza Firouzja secured Group A with two draws against Levon Aronian. Firouzja finishes on fifteen points, one ahead of Jan-Krzysztof Duda and Jorden van Foreest. Duda won their first encounter with White, but Van Foreest answered with a White victory in the return game. Both finish on fourteen points, with Duda taking second place and Van Foreest third on the Blitz tiebreak. Andrew Hong and Nodirbek Abdusattorov also drew twice. Hong finished on eleven points, level with Aronian, who took fourth place on the tiebreak. Hong is fifth and Abdusattorov sixth on nine. Caruana wins Group B despite final-round defeat Fabiano Caruana finished three points clear of the runner-up in Group B despite losing his final game to Vladislav Artemiev. After a draw in their opening encounter, Artemiev won the return with White to end Caruana’s unbeaten Fast Classic run. Caruana closes on seventeen points from four wins, five draws and one defeat. Le Quang Liem Le drew twice with Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu to finish second on fourteen points. Le completed all ten games unbeaten, with two wins and eight draws. Praggnanandhaa finishes sixth on seven. Richard Rapport and Vincent Keymer also drew both games. Rapport takes third place on eleven points, while Keymer finishes fourth on ten, ahead of Artemiev on the Blitz tiebreak. Giri seals first place as all six games are drawn Anish Giri’s two draws with Shakhriyar Mamedyarov were enough to secure first place in Group C on fifteen points. All six games in the group were drawn, leaving the standings unchanged. Mamedyarov finishes fourth on eleven. Ian Nepomniachtchi drew twice with Magnus Carlsen, while Haik Martirosyan and Abhimanyu Mishra also split points in both games. Nepomniachtchi and Martirosyan finished on thirteen, with the Blitz tiebreak placing Nepomniachtchi second and Martirosyan third. Carlsen ended up fifth on nine points after nine draws and one defeat, without a Fast Classic victory in the group stage. Mishra is sixth on eight. Vachier-Lagrave claims top spot as Vaishali defeats Erigaisi Maxime Vachier-Lagrave broke the three-way tie at the top of Group D with a win and a draw against Bibisara Assaubayeva. After drawing the opening game, he won the return with White in an endgame. His seventeen points secure first place, while Assaubayeva finished fifth on ten. Hans Moke Niemann recovered from a first-game loss to Wesley So by winning their return encounter with White. Niemann finished second on sixteen points, ahead of Erigaisi on the Blitz tiebreak, while So is fourth on thirteen. Vaishali Rameshbabu produced one of the day’s standout results by beating Arjun Erigaisi after losing their opening game. The return encounter swung both ways before Vaishali eventually secured the win. The split result leaves Erigaisi third with sixteen points and Vaishali sixth with seven. The players have a rest day on Monday, November 16, before the knockout semifinals begin on Tuesday, November 17. The Blitz seeding pairs Vachier-Lagrave with Giri and Firouzja with Caruana in the championship bracket. All 24 players continue in six knockout brackets, with matches combining Blitz, Rapid and Fast Classic. Text: Total Chess Photos: Maria Emelianova and Michal Walusza Official website: www.totalchess.com About Total Chess Total Chess is a global championship platform established to redefine elite competitive chess for the modern era. Developed by Norway Chess and approved by FIDE, the Total Chess World Championship Tour introduces a unified format that crowns the world’s ultimate champion by testing excellence across three disciplines: Fast Classical, Rapid and Blitz. The Tour will bring together the world’s top 24 men and women players to compete across four premier international events hosted in leading global cities. Designed to elevate the sport’s commercial appeal and fan engagement, Total Chess combines world-class competition with innovation, technology and immersive spectator experiences to create a new benchmark for professional chess. With a vision to make chess one of the world’s most engaging and commercially sustainable sports, Total Chess aims to expand the game’s global footprint, inspire the next generation of players, and connect millions of fans through a dynamic championship that celebrates intelligence, strategy and sporting excellence.

title: ChessBase 27: Ready for Launch!
summary:
The most important change in the new ChessBase 27 is that it has moved beyond being a traditional chess database program – it is becoming an integrated environment for opening preparation, chess training, coaching, engine analysis and AI-assisted research. New programming techniques have improved performance and stability, particularly in database searching, sorting and maintenance. And everything is noticeably faster. Take note of the launch date: November 17, 2027.

Like to get an impression of ChessBase 27 and what it can do to help you?

Click the above image to start a short video which will show you some of the main features that have been implemented in the latest version of our program.

And here is a summary of all the new functions ChessBase 27 and what they actually do:

The most important new features

1. The Opening Catalog

A new interactive opening encyclopedia built directly into the board window.

Around 2,000 opening entries, based on the ECO system.

Graphical profiles showing characteristics such as sharpness, draw tendency, central structure, branching complexity and endgame probability.

Opening articles explaining the history, ideas and current theoretical status of a variation.

Annotated repertoire recommendations for White and Black.

Audio narration, tactical puzzles and quizzes.

The catalog follows the position on the board. You can click a variation in an article to play it directly in the notation.

Why it matters: This is a major step towards integrating opening instruction, repertoire building and theoretical research into one interface.

2. Ask ChessBase

Probably the most ambitious new feature. It uses the Anthropic or OpenAI agentic interface which then accesses ChessBase functionality directly for very advanced AI interaction. This is vastly superior to discussing chess in a conventional AI chat window and a revolutionary way to study chess. Agentic AI interfaces today are usually associated with token costs. Premium users have FREE limited access until December 31, 2026. And if you already use an API key from Anthropic or OpenAI you can also bring this. Examples include:

Creating a complete fully annotated opening repertoire for a club player.

Analysing a game and producing (text) annotations that are equivalent to what a human would do

Preparing against a specific opponent according to your own repertoire

Building a database of important endgame positions for self study.

Suggested moves can be replayed on the board, and explanations can be presented as a visual walkthrough. Conversations can be saved locally and exported as PDFs with diagrams. Why it matters: This is a new way of interacting with a chess database. You can ask for a complete chess research task instead of manually navigating through databases, engines and notations.

3. The Coach System

A complete environment for live chess lessons. The coach starts a session and shares a link or QR code. Students can join using a free web application on a computer, tablet or phone.

Features include:

Demonstrating games and positions.

Seeing moves entered by individual students.

Switching between private, live and locked modes.

Allowing students to analyse independently.

Setting exercises and discussing them individually.

Audio and video communication.

Why it matters: ChessBase becomes a teaching platform, not just a database used by a chess coach.

4. Plans Explorer

A new tool for discovering typical strategic plans from a reference database.

It identifies recurring plans for both sides in the current position, lists the games in which they occurred and displays the relevant piece manoeuvres graphically on the board.

You can click on a plan to examine the games in which it was used.

Why it matters: It helps answer a question that ordinary opening statistics cannot: what are players actually tring to achieve in this position?

5. Lichess Tree

A new opening-tree pane based on more than eight billion Lichess games. It displays:

Moves played from the current position.

Frequencies and results.

Games reaching the position.

Filters for different time controls.

Separate trees for variants such as Chess960 and Atomic.

Why it matters: It gives access to a huge online playing database, with a different player population and playing environment from traditional tournament databases. We identify this as a Premium feature.

6. New analysis and training functions

Full Chess960 support. This is supported throughout the program, including opening books, tactical analysis, Buddy engine and Monte Carlo analysis.

Play against Fritz. ChessBase 27 l ets you play out a position against Fritz, using its human-play algorithm. Useful for honing positions in your repertoire.

Repertoire Training. A dedicated function for practicing your opening repertoire.

Analysis Board. This provides a second, independent board for exploring variations without changing the game being analysed.

Quick Annotation. You c an incorporate deep analysis from archived live broadcasts into game annotations.

Practical Engine Moves. This is a particularly interesting addition. The engine pane can now distinguish between:

The objectively best move.

Moves that are almost equally strong but create more practical problems.

Moves that leave the opponent with only one satisfactory reply.

The program marks the most practically attractive moves, and also provides a verbal assessment of how difficult a continuation is to find. This is useful when preparing against a particular opponent. The best practical move is not always the move with the highest engine evaluation.

7. Other new functions

Interesting Games. ChessBase 27 uses machine learning to assign an interest score to games. The system learns from features of annotated games in Mega Database and applies this knowledge to other games. The score appears in the game list and can be used for sorting.

CQL Search. The program supports Chess Query Language, allowing searches for specific chess patterns, tactical themes and endgame configurations. Examples:

Smothered mates.

Knight underpromotions.

Model mates.

Particular endgame configurations.

Games ending in stalemate between highly rated players.

This is a particularly powerful tool for chess historians, researchers and authors.

Raytracer board: This can be used to create photo realistic images of a chess position. In CB27 the stability, performance and look has been significantly improved. You immediately get a nice looking rendering of the position. Also it works well together with the new analysis board.

The launch of ChessBase 27 is on Tuesday, November 17!

Important Information on Usage

ChessBase Account and Installation: The software can be installed on up to three devices. The program can only be used with one ChessBase account.

Premium Membership: A valid Premium Membership is required to use the ChessBase’27 online features. A 12-month Premium Membership is included in the package.

Coach Feature: Usage is limited to one coach with up to 5 students and a total of 25 teaching hours per month.

Ask ChessBase (AI Assistant): Usage is charged in Ducats. During the introductory period until December 31, 2026, usage worth up to 100 Ducats per week is free of charge. Once this free allowance has been used up, users must spend their own Ducats, which can be purchased if needed. From January 1, 2027, usage will be charged from the start.
